analysis.one_liner: Sends every family a monthly check per child, ending the child tax credit and EITC.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on November 20, 2025, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The End Child Poverty Act would create a new program run through the Social Security Administration that mails a monthly payment to the family of every child under 19 living in the U.S. The payment equals the difference between the federal poverty guideline for a two-person household and for a single person — roughly $500 a month per child, adjusted each year. Families would be signed up automatically using IRS and Social Security records unless they opt out. In exchange, the bill ends the Child Tax Credit and the Earned Income Tax Credit and replaces them with two new tax credits: $700 per adult dependent, and $700 for every adult aged 19 to 64 ($1,400 for a married couple), phasing out for higher incomes.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children under 19, especially low- and middle-income ones, who would get a guaranteed monthly payment with no work or earnings requirement. Parents caring for adult dependents over 18, and adults aged 19 to 64, would also receive new credits. The payments would not count as income for taxes or reduce eligibility for other federal benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a universal monthly child payment for every child under 19, sized off the poverty guidelines and adjusted annually, with annual true-up payments when guidelines are updated mid-year.

Enrolls children automatically by treating Social Security number applications and IRS-identified dependents as applications unless the family opts out, so the poorest families do not have to navigate paperwork to get paid.

Replaces the Child Tax Credit and Earned Income Tax Credit with refundable credits of $700 for adult dependents and $700 ($1,400 joint) for adults aged 19 to 64, phasing out above $20,000 of income for singles and $40,000 for couples.

The payments are disregarded as income for taxes and for eligibility for other federal, state, and locally financed programs, so receiving them cannot cost a family food assistance, housing help, or Medicaid.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally: the bill sets up a large new entitlement and does not include an offset to pay for it. Families that rely on the Earned Income Tax Credit's extra reward for working — including single workers without children — would lose that credit and get a smaller, flatter replacement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; some working families losing the EITC

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the Earned Income Tax Credit entirely for tax years after 2025, which today supplements wages for low- and moderate-income workers and encourages work; the new flat $700 adult credit is smaller for many single working parents and removes the credit's work-linked phase-in.
The bill includes no funding source or deficit offset for the new child payments or the new adult credits; the cost would be added to federal borrowing or require a later funding vote.

Automatic enrollment depends on a new IRS data-sharing provision that lets the Social Security Administration receive taxpayer information — including children's citizenship status and country of residence — to identify eligible children, raising privacy and data-security questions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a low-income family with children, the monthly payment would be far larger than the current Child Tax Credit and arrives without needing to file taxes, which is a real gain, and the income disregard protects other benefits. The honest cost is on the other side of the ledger: ending the EITC trades a proven wage supplement with a strong work incentive for a flat payment, the bill's costs are unfunded, and the adult credits are modest. The design is a deliberate trade of work-linked tax benefits for universal cash aid, and that trade has genuine defenders and critics.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the End Child Poverty Act in the House on November 20, 2025, with seven original co-introducers.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax credits.
The bill has 10 cosponsors, all Democrats, and the committee action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody has won or lost yet — the bill is sitting in committee. If it follows the pattern of earlier versions of this proposal, the families who would have received the payments are the ones left waiting, while the current tax code stays as it is for taxpayers and the tax-preparation industry alike.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Child Poverty Act and led its introduction in the House.

for.name: Reps. Norton, Lee of Pennsylvania, McIver, Omar, Thanedar, Watson Coleman, and Pressley
for.what_they_did: Joined as original co-sponsors at introduction; the bill drew 10 Democratic cosponsors in total.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred — no hearing or markup has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors plus the sponsor are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and Republicans hold the majority on the committee where the bill sits.

industries.note: Today, families often pay preparers or software companies to claim refundable credits like the EITC on their tax returns. The bill would pay most families automatically through Social Security records without a return, shrinking the tax-filing business tied to those credits.

The bill creates a large new spending program and a new SSA office with no offsetting revenue, while ending the two largest refundable tax credits. The net cost would fall on federal borrowing or future taxpayers.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress is in session through early 2027, but the bill's realistic path is a quiet end: versions of this same proposal introduced in prior Congresses never got a committee vote, and with only Democratic cosponsors and a Republican-led Ways and Means Committee, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote this session.
